title: Too Good
passages:
The shackle was a seized pin in a rusted body, and it would have taken ten minutes with a hammer and a punch and a man who didn't mind losing skin. Sol didn't have ten minutes. She had the deck torch instead — a bottle of oxygen, a hose, and a steel pipe that burned a hole in anything you pointed it at — and she put the flame on the pin until the pin went white, then yellow, then let go, and six years of the Marrow tied to the transit station went down into the harbor in one long bright link at a time.

"You just set fire to six years," Wren said.

"I set fire to a pin." Sol killed the torch and racked it. "Six years is a number. Dey!"

Dey came up the deck with the axe. Twenty minutes out of the recompression box — the steel tube they'd pressurized to squeeze the fizz back into his blood — and he was still bent, still walking like a man on gravel in bare feet, and he took the axe off the rack and set his feet and knocked the last pinched link off the fairlead in two swings. Sparks went into the water and drowned.

"Show-off," Wren said.

"He's paid by the hour," Sol said. "Cast off."

The Marrow came off the station and swung her bow into the current, and Wren went to the storm glass for the number. The storm glass was a sealed tube of camphor and salt water that clouded as the air pressure dropped, so you could read the weather at arm's length instead of trusting a forecast. It had clouded two marks since dawn.

"Eight hours forty," she said.

"That's not nine."

"No. It's eight forty."

Sol said something about the Factor's mother that Wren chose not to put in the log.

"Course?"

"Zero-four-zero. The Mercy's bearing."

Sol took the wheel in both hands and held it like it owed her something. The Mercy General was six kilometers out, a hospital tower with its top nine floors in the air and the rest of it in the water, and the bearing to it ran across open chop the whole way. She pulled the grease pencil from behind her ear and wrote zero-four-zero on the back of her left hand, in the strip of skin below the thumb where she kept her numbers. There were older numbers there already, layered over each other in the same wax, some of them smudged to gray ghosts where her palm had dragged through them.

Wren looked at the old ones a beat too long. Sol put the hand in her jacket pocket.

"Log it," Sol said.

Wren logged it. Then she looked back at the glass, because the glass was where the argument lived, and the cloud had come up another mark while she stood there — a third of the tube gone white in the time it took to write a course.

"Eight hours forty," she said again, and heard how it sounded, and said it anyway.

Sol didn't look at the glass. She looked at the water ahead, and then at Dey, who had racked the axe and was standing at the rail with his weight on his heels like a man who'd forgotten he was hurt.

"Below," Sol said. "Both of you. I want the sled packed before we're in sight."

Dey went. Wren stayed one second longer at the glass, watching the white climb, and did the arithmetic she was going to have to do out loud in about four minutes, and hated every digit of it.

Below, the cabin was low and hot off the engine and crowded with everything the Marrow owned and never threw away. Dey had the suit to his waist already. Wren went to the bench, took his slate off its hook — a rubber-cased unit that logged his depth and his gas and ran the boat's voice into the bone of his jaw so topside could talk to him down there — and clamped it over the seal at his wrist.

"Give me your thumb," Dey said, and put his hand out, and she didn't take it.

On the slate's face was a line for the sign-off, the place where the topside tech certified a diver fit for the depth he was going to. Fifty-two. Her thumb had never once left that line blank.

"I'm not signing you," Wren said.

"For the case?"

"For any of it past forty." She turned the slate so he could see the empty line. "My thumb there says you're fit and it says I'll build you back if you're not, and I've done it a hundred times, and I'm not doing it to you at fifty-two."

"You did it to me yesterday."

"I cut you an hour yesterday and you kept the part I cut." She heard her own voice climb and didn't fix it. "That's the whole problem, Dey. It doesn't stay cut."

Sol came down the ladder, leaving the wheel to hold its own heading, into the middle of it. "Reader signs or Reader doesn't, we're on the Mercy in six hours. Pick."

"Then send me." Wren held the slate out like a warrant. "I'm rated to forty. I'll take the tether, I'll bring the case up, and he sits in the box where I can watch him."

"No." Sol didn't look at the slate.

"I'm the only one aboard who can put a man back together and you'd keep me on the bench—"

"That's exactly why." Sol took the slate out of her hand and hung it back on the hook, gentle, which was worse than if she'd thrown it. "You're the only one who can put him back. So you're the one stays dry. You go in the water and crack your head on a doorframe, then who builds him? Dey? You want Dey stitching a man's hours back with a boat manual?"

"I want Dey to have a man to stitch."

The engine filled the space where Sol didn't answer.

"You're not trading a case," Wren said, quieter, because quiet carried further down here. "Twelve thousand buys five berths on the high ground. I did the arithmetic — I do it every hour. You're not buying berths with the Factor's money. You're buying them with him." She pointed at Dey without looking, the way you point at weather. "You'll spend a nineteen-year-old's whole head for a dry bunk, and you'll do it because you can't remember you already spent your own the same way."

Sol's jaw worked. When she spoke it was even. "You cut Ivo Salas out of him and he kept it anyway. You've built every man on this crew back wrong on purpose so he'd sleep. Don't stand on my deck and price my trade when your whole job is deciding what people are allowed to know they did."

"Reader," Dey said.

Neither of them looked at him.

"I know what you cut," Dey said. "I kept it. Ivo lent me air at forty-two and he's still down there, and you both know it." He pulled the suit up over his shoulders and reached for the ring at his throat, unhurried, a man getting dressed for work. "So you can stand here and price each other, or one of you can come wind the winch."

He sealed the ring. The slate on his wrist chirped once, waiting for the thumbprint that would let him past forty, and Wren's hand was still empty, and above them the storm glass climbed another mark in the dark.

"Get the mix," Wren said.

Dey looked at the slate chirping on his wrist, then at her, and went forward.

He came back with the first bottle upright in both arms, bent at the waist, setting his feet down like a man crossing gravel barefoot, and walked it into the rack at the back of the sled. The sled was a welded steel skid about the size of a door: a cradle in the middle shaped to take the cold-case, a lifting ring at the nose for the tether, gas racked behind.

"White bands," Dey said, reading the shoulder. "Trimix."

"Oxygen, nitrogen, helium," Wren said. "Helium's so you don't get drunk at fifty-two. Oxygen's cut low so it doesn't burn you. Air would've been a fifth the price and you'd be a comedian on the bottom."

"I'm a comedian up here."

"You're a *dent* up here."

The second bottle went in beside the first. She read both gauges out loud, because a man ought to hear his own air before he trusts it in the dark.

"Three hundred bar each. Call it forty-one minutes of breathing. Thirty-eight if you dawdle, and you dawdle." She swung the rack bar down and dropped the pin through it. "There's no second set."

"No second set," Sol said from the ladder.

"Because the second set is twelve hundred and a berth is twenty-four hundred, and the Factor's advance went into these two and the diesel."

Overhead the deck chain went slack and started to rattle, and Sol came down with the green bottle in one hand, the mask still bagged and zip-tied to the valve, the clear hose coiled over her forearm.

She clamped it to the sled with two hose clamps and ran a lanyard through the ring, then stood back and looked at her work.

Wren stood up off the bench.

"That's the recompression bottle."

"It's reserve."

"It's oxygen under pressure on a full-face mask, two hours of it, and it's the reason he walked out of that box yesterday instead of being carried out." She kept her voice flat and clear, the voice she used for the log. "Say whose hide that's paid out of. Out loud. Slate's running."

Sol wiped her hands down her thighs. "Reserve is reserve."

"There's a steel tube in the lazarette with a hand pump and nothing to pump. He comes up bent, there is nothing on this boat that puts him back." Wren put her thumb flat on the slate's face — not the sign-off line, just the glass, over the count. "So you'd spend the one thing that would've, on a box."

"I'd spend it on five bunks."

"Then log it: one recompression bottle, out of Dey Okafor, twelve thousand."

"Log it as reserve gas."

"That's the same sentence with his name off it."

Dey took the other end of the green bottle before either of them could get a hand on it, and walked it forward, and set it in the clamps.

"Heavy for air," he said.

"It's not air."

"Nothing aboard this boat is what the label says." He threaded the lanyard, cinched it down, and patted the bottle twice, cheerful as a man loading groceries. "Forty-one minutes, Reader. I'll be up before you've finished being right."

Which was worse than if he'd argued.

She held out her hand and he gave her his wrist, and she keyed the cert line and put her thumb down and wrote *40* in the depth field.

Dey read it upside down. "That's not fifty-two."

"No. The slate alarms at whatever I certify, so above forty it stops telling me anything at all. I'll call your depth and your mix myself, every minute, by voice." She let go of his wrist. "Past forty you're off my log with nothing behind you but your word, and your word is what I'd have to build you out of."

"Fair," Dey said, and meant it, and that was the part she liked least.

She turned to lash the bottle down against the cradle, and the drone came down out of the chop and hung off the portlight, near enough that Wren could see herself in the lens, bent around the curve of it. It held there the whole time Dey sealed the second bottle, and then it went back up, unhurried, the way a thing goes when it has already counted what it came to count.

Wren watched it climb. Then she looked at the green bottle clamped where the treatment used to live, and at the empty bracket swinging on its chain over the deck.

"Thirty-eight," she said, to nobody, "if he dawdles."

The harbor chop ended about a kilometer out, where the breakwater used to be, and after that it was building sea: long gray swell out of the northeast with the tops starting to tear, six kilometers of it between the Marrow and the Mercy. She went up each face, hung at the top with her screw out of the water and screaming, and dropped, and everything on deck that wasn't lashed went looking for the rail.

The Factor's drone held station off the port bow at eye height — two meters off the water, which is eye height for a thing that flies — and didn't wobble once, not in that sea, which meant it was spending money to stay there.

"Course," Sol said.

"Zero-four-zero."

"Good." Sol squinted past the bow at nothing Wren could see. "Hate to burn a season's diesel pointed at the wrong building."

"You'd find something in it. You always do."

Dey sat on the sled with his fins across his knees, running the tether through his hands a meter at a time. The tether was the line that would run from the boat to his harness the whole way down and back, so topside could haul and he could feel the haul. He was looking for the soft flat place a chafe leaves before it parts.

The Mercy came up out of the weather at four kilometers. Nine dry floors standing in the air with the waterline crossing the building below them at a slant, empty window sockets in rows, and on the third dry deck the helipad with an ambulance still on it, doors open, one wheel chocked with a brick somebody had carried up there for the purpose.

Sol wiped her mouth with the back of her right hand and looked at the left one.

"Course?"

"Zero-four-zero. It was zero-four-zero ten minutes ago. It'll be zero-four-zero when we're alongside, unless you've turned the boat."

"It's a bearing, not a lottery." Sol put the wheel over two spokes to meet a swell and took it back. "I like hearing it in your voice. You've got a good voice for numbers."

"I've got a good voice for everything. That's the tragedy of my life."

Wren let it sit for one swell. Then she didn't.

"I'll take the approach," she said. "You go below, put your feet up for ten minutes, I'll bring her onto the helipad and call the bearing off the tower mast, and you can come up after and tell me every single thing I did wrong."

Sol's hands closed on the wheel. The tendons stood up on the backs of them and the knuckles went the color of the grease pencil.

"You want the helm."

"I want you off your feet."

"You want the *helm*." Loud enough that Dey looked up off the tether. "I bought this boat off a man who drowned in her. She's mine while I'm standing on her deck, and nobody aboard takes her wheel while I'm standing on her deck."

"Fine."

"Fine."

The drone slid in a meter, unhurried, the way a thing moves when it has all day and somebody is paying for it.

Sol breathed out. When she spoke again it came flat and fast, a woman reading a gauge off a wall.

"Dey. Numbers, not warnings. You forget warnings, you forget everything. Thirty takes the hour — you come up and an hour's gone out of you and it doesn't come back, and it doesn't hurt going, that's the trick of it."

"Thirty takes the hour."

"Forty takes names and faces. Not the ones you're thinking of now. The ones you'd die for. Then their faces go, and you stay calm, and you tell me you're fine in a voice I don't know."

"Forty takes names and faces."

"Fifty takes the surface." Sol turned all the way around. "Not that it's far. You stop believing up is a place. And you'll be reasonable about it. You'll explain it to me."

Dey nodded slow, the way a man nods at a price he's decided to pay.

"And past fifty?"

"There is no past fifty. Fifty's the wall. You go to fifty-two because the Factor's box is sitting at fifty-two, and there's twelve thousand in it, and one year of you." She turned back to the water. "You touch that case and you're on the tether, and I don't care what your voice sounds like when you tell me you're fine."

"Copy," Dey said, and went back to the line.

Two kilometers. The swell had started breaking white on the base of the tower, and the Marrow's bow came down hard enough to slam the deck plates, and Sol rode it with her knees and didn't move her hands.

"Good," she said. "And when we get alongside, you remind me what it is we're lifting."

"Cold-case," Dey said. "Medical. Factor's seal on the lid, ward four, fifty-two meters. Twelve thousand on the helipad, and the drone counts seals before anybody cuts a wire."

"Good. Say it again when we're alongside and I'll believe it."

"Captain." He didn't raise his voice. He'd stopped running the tether through his hands. "The salvage tower's four hundred meters off your line. That's not a detour, that's a rounding error. Two hours, one ride on the winch, and Ivo Salas breathes gas that isn't his own spit. Then I'll go get your box."

Sol didn't slow. The Marrow came off a swell, hung, slammed down, and she rode it with her knees and never moved her hands.

"No."

"He's in a bubble the size of a coffin lid—"

"He's in a bubble he chose, four hundred meters the wrong way, on a boat that's got eight hours of weather in it." She tipped the wheel a spoke to meet the next one. "Two hours over, an hour on the winch, an hour back. Then the glass is white and we're tied to a chimney with five aboard and no berth. Five, Dey. Not one."

"So he's a rounding error."

"So are you, and I like you better." No heat in it at all, which was worse than heat. "You walked out of that box twenty minutes ago like a man crossing gravel barefoot and you want me to put you down another tower before you've had something hot. That's not saving a man. That's posting him."

"Copy," Dey said.

Wren watched his hands, because his hands had stopped looking for chafe.

The spare tether lived coiled on the sled nose — thirty meters of line thin as a bootlace, for hauling a bag up when a diver's arms are full of something else. The winch toggle was the T-pin that drops out of the deck winch drum; pull it and two hundred meters of cable pays out with nothing on God's earth slowing it. Neither had any business inside a suit.

He palmed the coil. He walked the toggle out of its bracket with his thumb, easy as taking a sweet off a child, and both went into the thigh pouch, and he pressed the flap down twice.

Wren opened her mouth and shut it. You do not stop a diver who has decided, not with a sentence. You keep a voice on him and you take his word for the rest.

"Reader." He was watching her watch him. "You saw that."

"I saw a man tidy his kit."

"Then tidy it in the log too." He held the wrist out, slate chirping at forty, waiting. "Play me all of it when I'm up. Whatever I did down there. Especially the part where I don't come when you call."

"That's not a favor, that's my job."

"It's not, though." He said it kindly, which was the annoying thing about him. "You cut Ivo out of me and kept him in your pocket, and you'd have kept him there forever if I hadn't gone and got him back. That's not a Reader. That's a landlord."

"Landlords don't work nights."

"You work every night."

Wren took his wrist and keyed the cert line and put her thumb down and wrote *40*, and then she said the rest of it out loud, in the flat voice she used for the log, because a price said quietly is a price nobody paid.

"New terms. I don't touch your slate. Not a splice, not a trim, not ever. You get every hour you earn down there, whole, and you get Ivo's name back on the top of the build where you can see it." She let go. "And when I give you three tugs, you come up."

"Three tugs and I come up."

"Say it on the slate."

"Three tugs and I come up," Dey said, to the slate, and the slate took it, and Wren logged it under his name and hers, and that was the first honest line she'd written on that unit in four years.

"Two kilometers," she said. "Helipad's clear, ambulance isn't going anywhere."

"Course," Sol said.

"Zero-four-zero. It's been zero-four-zero since the transit station."

"I like hearing it in your voice."

Sol put the wheel over, and the Mercy stopped being a shape and became a building — nine dry floors, the waterline cutting across the tenth at a slant, empty window sockets in rows. The drone slid off the bow and took up station over the helipad like it had paid for the parking. Wren went below for the winch cable and came back with it over her shoulder and heard Sol, forward, stop.

"Reader." Sol's voice was odd. "Where's the pin?"

The winch drum's ear was two feet from Wren's hand, a steel tab with a hole in it, and the hole was empty.

"Which pin," she said.

"The one that stops two hundred meters of cable going over the side at the speed of falling." Sol hadn't raised her voice. She saved that for weather.

"It walked out at the station. Everything on this boat walks out at the station, it's the vibration." Wren was already moving. "Ninety seconds."

The ambulance had been dead long enough for its tires to take the shape of the deck. She reached past the open rear doors and pulled the hood rod out of its clips under the dash — a bent steel rod with a flattened, drilled end, built in a factory to hold an engine lid up while a man looked at an engine — laid it across the deck edge, and hit it twice with the poll of the axe. It parted. She kept the half with the hole and drove it through the ear.

"Somebody's last emergency," Sol said, "and you're robbing it."

"They're not using it."

Sol brought the Marrow in on short bursts, and Wren took two lines onto the helipad, one around the ambulance's chassis and one around a stanchion, and the fenders squealed down the tower's flank until the boat lay against the third dry floor with a hand's width of chop between hull and concrete.

The stairwell was amidships under a hatch, and it went down the spine of the building like a shaft. Wren got the hatch up and the smell came out, and then the water, which did not move the way harbor water moves. It stood black and rose the width of a hand and sank again, patient, like something asleep in there.

Dey sat on the sill with his fins on and his slate chirping at forty. She read his gauges out loud a second time, because a man ought to hear his own air twice.

"Marks on the line every ten meters, wax and a cable tie. I call them as they go under. At thirty you swap — the bottle on your back is shallow mix, more oxygen in it for warm water, and past thirty it's too rich and it'll convulse you. So you come onto the sled bottle and you clip the shallow one back in the rack. Say it."

"Thirty, swap, clip back."

"Go."

He went over the sill backwards, and the black took him to the chest, and then he was gone and the cable ran and his breathing came up through the bone of Wren's jaw, close and unhurried, with the tick of the exhaust under it. The green bottle rode down ahead of him on the sled, clamped where the treatment used to live.

"Ten," she said. "Twenty."

The depth field on the slate sat at forty and would sit there all day. Past forty she had a wax mark on a wet rope and her own voice.

"Thirty. Swap."

The pitch of his breathing changed as he came onto the deep mix. Then, "Reader."

"Go."

"It's quiet down here." A pause with nothing in it. "Is it quiet up there?"

"Full of noise. Focus."

"I'm focused."

"Captain," Sol said. "Bearing."

"Zero-four-zero. Third time."

"Give it to me again."

"Sol." Wren kept one hand on the cable, feeling for the next tie. "The helipad's dead ahead, the ambulance is on it, and the tower's not going anywhere. You could steer this boat with your knees and a grudge."

The cable went over the side. Somewhere behind her Sol's boots came two steps along the deck and stopped.

"I can't read the hand," Sol said.

Wren turned around.

"The strip below the thumb. Grease pencil, six years of it. I put a number there and by the time I need it the sweat's taken it or my palm has, and I stand at the wheel and pick a heading and hope the building's where I left it." Sol's voice was flat and quick, a woman reading a gauge off a wall. "Two years, give or take. I know what it is. Same as Dey's got, only I've been buying it in installments."

"Say the rest."

"I won't hand the wheel over because a boat whose captain can't read her own hand isn't mine, it's whoever's holding it." She looked at Wren. "You want to hear it on the log, put it on the log."

Wren keyed the slate. "Captain Sol Ferreira, on the record, cannot read her own depth marks and has not since two years back. Witnessed, Wren Achebe." She let go of the key. "You could've said that at the transit station and saved me a fight."

"I don't like fights I win."

"You didn't win that one."

"No." Sol almost smiled. "Ask me again when we're tied up."

"Reader." Dey's voice, slow, agreeable. "It's very quiet."

Wren's hand went flat on the cable. Thirty-four meters, at the speed that line was paying out, and he was talking like a man at forty.

"Captain. He's four meters past the switch with the forty voice."

"How slow."

"Slow and patient and polite. Say haul."

Sol's thumb found the winch brake and stayed on it.

"He's got twenty meters of work."

Wren put her own hand over Sol's on the brake, and neither of them moved it.

Wren took her hand off the brake.

"Say the number," Sol said.

"Thirty-four. Thirty-six." Wren's palm lay flat on the cable, reading the wax ties as they came up through her fingers, cold and gritty. "Thirty-eight. Forty. He's on the bottom mix and I've got no more marks, so from here it's arithmetic and his word."

"Then do the arithmetic out loud so I can hear you do it."

"Forty-two."

"Reader."

"Go."

"There's a door off the shaft and the door's open and there's a trolley in the way and I'm going around it." A long pause with the tick of the exhaust in it. "Forty-six."

"Forty-eight."

"Reader, there's a room with four beds in it and the mattresses are gone and the frames are white, and it's warm."

"It's not warm. You're on helium, it's fifty-one degrees down there and it's going to feel like a bakery."

"It's warm." He said it kindly. "Fifty."

"Fifty-one."

The line came up with the slow steady weight of a man walking. Then it stopped.

"Fifty-two." She looked at Sol. "He's on the bottom."

"Say your name," Sol said, to the water.

"Case," Dey said.

"Say your *name*, Dey."

"There's a case on its side in the middle of the floor. Green paint, white stencils, the Factor's seal wired at both corners. It's got a window in the lid, about so big, and the frost is on the inside of the glass." A pause. "The seal's a year old. Somebody's rewired it."

"Say your name."

"It's warm in here and the frost's on the inside." He said it patiently, the way you'd explain a thing to a child who keeps asking. "Reader. How do you carry a boat?"

Wren looked at Sol. Sol's hand was flat on the brake and her face had gone the color of the deck.

"Give him three tugs," Sol said. "Now."

Wren took the cable in both hands, braced a boot on the coaming, and pulled: one long, two short, spaced out so he'd feel each one come down the line. The marks ran through her fists. Nothing came back up.

"He hasn't taken them."

"Again."

She hauled again, harder, and this time she got an answer — not three tugs. A bump, like something knocking on a wall two streets over.

"Reader," Dey said. "What's up?"

"You're on the tether. Up is the tether. Up is one kilometer of wet rope in my two hands and a woman with her thumb on the winch, and you put your hand on the line and you come up it."

"Up is where the Reader is."

"Up is where I am. Come up it."

"That's what I thought." A pause, unhurried, the pause of a man considering something in good light. "I'm going to the case now. It's only eight meters."

Overhead the drone slid down off the helipad, dropped through the hatch, and hung a meter above Wren's head, lens down, counting seals.

"Eight meters," Sol said. "Mark your line."

There was no sound at all for three seconds. Then the line came up slack and light in Wren's fists, all the weight gone out of it, and started to pay out again sideways, fast, smooth, the way line runs when a man is swimming with his hands free.

"He's off the tether," she said.

"Take up the slack and haul him in."

"He unclipped, Sol, he's swimming and there's no line on him—"

"Then take up the slack and *haul*—"

The breathing stopped.

Not cut off. Stopped, like a man setting down a heavy box and straightening up to look at the room.

Wren's hands were full of dead rope. "Dey. Dey, breathe on my count. One. Two."

Nothing. Then the flat crack of a glove on a steel wall, four times, unhurried, like a man knocking at a house where he's expected.

"He's knocking on the case," she said.

"Reader." His voice again, and it was the worst voice yet, warm and conversational, a man talking across a kitchen table. "There's a face behind the frost."

"Whose face?"

"It's a girl's face and she's got her hand on a crank." He sounded delighted. "She's been winding it. Reader, she's got a *hand* on it, going round and round, and there's a little boy in the bottom half with a mask on and the glass is all steamed where he's been breathing, and she's saying—"

Under his voice, on the bone track, thin and small and clear as a wire, a girl's voice said, "Teo, hold on. Hold on, I've got it, I've got it—" and then, to Dey, not frightened, only flat and tired and certain: "You're not him. You're not Ivo Salas."

Wren's hand was already on the slate, thumbing for the key.
